title: Week 2 · Lesson 6: Tissue Repair, Wound Healing & Fibrosis — FNP-Level Approach
html:
PHASE 1 · ADVANCED PATHOPHYSIOLOGY + CLINICAL REASONING

Week 2 — Lesson 6: Tissue Repair, Wound Healing & Fibrosis

FNP-level goal: Explain how tissue repairs itself, recognize why wounds fail to heal, and make safe decisions about infection, ischemia, pressure injury, diabetes, and referral urgency.

Learning Objectives

  • Distinguish regeneration from fibrosis.
  • Explain the overlapping phases of wound healing.
  • Apply macrophage, fibroblast, angiogenesis, and collagen mechanisms to clinical findings.
  • Build a differential for chronic lower-extremity wounds.
  • Recognize wound and limb-threatening red flags.

Part 1 — Repair Has Two Possible Outcomes

Regeneration restores tissue using cells of the same type when the injury is limited and the cellular/extracellular-matrix framework is preserved.

Fibrosis replaces damaged tissue with extracellular matrix and collagen. It helps preserve structural integrity but can reduce normal organ function.

Severity of injury + regenerative capacity + matrix integrity + persistence of inflammation determine the outcome.

Part 2 — The Four Overlapping Phases

Hemostasis → inflammation → proliferation → remodeling. These are overlapping processes, not four isolated days on a calendar.

Hemostasis: vasoconstriction, platelet activation, coagulation, and a fibrin clot stop bleeding and provide a provisional scaffold.

Inflammation: neutrophils and then macrophages clear organisms and debris. Appropriate inflammation supports healing; persistent inflammation delays healing and promotes fibrosis.

Proliferation: fibroblasts produce matrix/collagen, endothelial cells form vessels, keratinocytes re-epithelialize, and granulation tissue develops.

Remodeling: collagen and matrix are reorganized; the scar becomes stronger but typically does not return to normal tissue architecture or strength.

Part 3 — Cells That Matter

Platelets: hemostasis plus early repair signaling.

Macrophages: debris clearance and transition from inflammation to repair; they coordinate cytokines and growth-factor signals.

Fibroblasts/myofibroblasts: extracellular matrix and collagen production; wound contraction.

Endothelial cells: angiogenesis, which supplies oxygen and nutrients to healing tissue.

Keratinocytes: re-epithelialization across the wound surface.

Part 4 — Oxygen and Perfusion

Healing requires ATP, immune function, collagen synthesis, cell migration, and angiogenesis. All depend on adequate oxygen delivery.

Poor arterial perfusion → oxygen delivery ↓ → cell function/collagen synthesis/host defense ↓ → delayed healing and tissue loss risk.

This connects Lesson 1 cellular injury to chronic wounds: a nonhealing wound is often a perfusion, pressure, neuropathy, infection, nutrition, or systemic-disease problem—not simply a dressing problem.

Part 5 — Primary vs Secondary Intention

Primary intention: clean, closely approximated wound edges; less tissue gap, less granulation tissue, and generally less scar.

Secondary intention: larger/open tissue defect; more granulation, contraction, matrix deposition, and scar. Some contaminated or infected wounds cannot safely be closed immediately.

Part 6 — Why Wounds Become Chronic

Local contributors: infection, biofilm/foreign material, inadequate perfusion, edema, repetitive trauma, pressure, large tissue loss, and poor off-loading.

Systemic contributors: diabetes, smoking, malnutrition, anemia, kidney/liver disease, immunosuppression, advanced age, and medications that affect healing.

Persistent injury → persistent inflammation → fibroblast activation + excess matrix deposition → fibrosis and impaired function.

Part 7 — Diabetes and the Foot

Diabetes can combine neuropathy, peripheral arterial disease, hyperglycemia-related host-defense impairment, and repetitive pressure/trauma.

Neuropathy → loss of protective sensation → unnoticed trauma.

PAD → perfusion ↓ → oxygen delivery ↓.

Hyperglycemia/immune dysfunction → infection risk and impaired repair.

FNP assessment should include wound location/size/depth, drainage/odor, surrounding erythema, pain, temperature, pulses, capillary refill/perfusion, edema, sensation, footwear/pressure points, systemic symptoms, glycemic context, and prior ulcers/amputations.

Part 8 — Lower-Extremity Wound Differential

Arterial/ischemic: distal distribution, reduced pulses, cool skin, pain or tissue loss; poor perfusion is the key mechanism.

Venous: edema and venous hypertension create an unfavorable tissue environment; often associated with lower-leg skin changes.

Neuropathic/diabetic: pressure-point injury with reduced protective sensation.

Pressure injury: sustained external pressure causes local ischemia, especially over bony prominences.

Infectious: cellulitis, abscess, deeper soft-tissue infection, or osteomyelitis may coexist with any of the above.

More than one mechanism is common. A “diabetic ulcer” may also be ischemic, infected, and pressure-related.

Part 9 — Infection and Limb-Threatening Red Flags

Escalate urgently for systemic toxicity, rapidly spreading erythema, severe/disproportionate pain, crepitus, bullae, skin necrosis, new sensory/motor deficit, absent/cool pulses, rest pain with tissue loss, deep wound/visible bone, suspected osteomyelitis, or inability to safely manage the wound outpatient.

Do not delay emergency evaluation for suspected necrotizing infection or acute limb ischemia while trying routine wound products.

Part 10 — Fibrosis Beyond Skin

Repeated injury in liver, kidney, lung, and heart can produce fibroblast activation, collagen deposition, distortion of normal architecture, and organ dysfunction.

Chronic injury → inflammation/repair signaling → extracellular matrix accumulation → fibrosis → loss of functional tissue.

This explains why chronic hepatitis can progress to cirrhosis, chronic kidney injury to nephron loss, and abnormal pulmonary repair to restrictive physiology and dyspnea.

Part 11 — Diagnostics and Management Principles

Testing should answer a question: Is there ischemia, infection, bone involvement, venous disease, pressure/neuropathy, systemic illness, or a contributor such as hyperglycemia/anemia/malnutrition?

Management targets cause: optimize perfusion assessment/referral, off-load pressure, manage edema when appropriate, control glycemia and infection, support nutrition, stop tobacco exposure, and arrange wound/vascular/podiatry/surgical involvement based on risk and scope.

Do not use compression, debridement, antibiotics, or closure as a generic response without assessing wound etiology and perfusion.

Part 12 — Board-Style Case 1

A patient with diabetes has a plantar ulcer beneath a pressure point, reduced sensation, no fever, and recurrent callus.

Mechanism: loss of protective sensation plus repetitive pressure/trauma; evaluate for perfusion and infection as co-contributors.

FNP next step: complete neurovascular and wound assessment, pressure/off-loading strategy, glycemic context, and appropriate referral/follow-up rather than treating the surface alone.

Part 13 — Board-Style Case 2

A patient has a chronic foot wound with new fever, rapidly expanding erythema, severe pain, and dusky skin.

FNP decision: possible deep/necrotizing infection and threatened tissue—emergency evaluation, not routine dressing change or delayed oral-treatment follow-up.

FNP High-Yield Framework

Healing: hemostasis → inflammation → proliferation → remodeling.

Macrophage: cleanup + repair coordination; fibroblast: collagen/matrix; angiogenesis: new vessels.

Chronic wound: ask perfusion, pressure, neuropathy, edema/venous disease, infection, and systemic contributors.

FNP decision: define the cause, document neurovascular status, treat modifiable contributors, and escalate promptly for infection, ischemia, systemic illness, or limb threat.
